question: What does it mean to establish prayer?

positions.position: Perform the prescribed prayers fully, with their required acts and at their appointed times.
positions.reasons: Al-Tabrisi and Ibn al-Jawzi specify complete bowing and prostration. Alusi includes regular observance or prayer at the beginning of its time. Jishumi says the verse fixes times generally while the Prophet explained details; Asad and Qurtubi likewise refer forms and exact times to prophetic teaching.

positions.position: Maintain prayer continuously, evenly, or at its best times.
positions.reasons: These are alternative glosses reported by al-Tabrisi and Abu Hayyan; al-Alusi also reports regular maintenance and beginning-of-time performance.

positions.position: Fill one's time with obligatory and voluntary worship or remembrance.
positions.reasons: Sufi authorities take the command to cover all time. Asad extends its stress on prayer to remembrance throughout waking life. Bursevi allows work, human needs, and restorative sleep.

positions.position: The five prayers close the five sensory doors and restore presence with God.
positions.reasons: Qashani says the senses veil the heart; praying at day edges preserves gathered light through intervening times (23:9), while night wakefulness refines powers drawn toward sleep.

positions.position: Prayer is the foremost worship after faith and a refuge in hardship.
positions.reasons: Razi relates its placement after steadfastness to its rank; Biqai calls it the broadest aid to uprightness; Qurtubi reports the Prophet turned to prayer when troubled.

question: Which prayers are at the two ends of the day?

positions.position: Fajr at the first end and Zuhr and Asr at the second.
positions.reasons: Wahidi prefers Zajjaj: Maghrib belongs to night. Zamakhshari calls Zuhr and Asr evening prayers; Elmalili calls them the after-noon division. Tabatabai says the five-prayer report points to before and after noon. Qurtubi reports Ibn Atiyya's choice. Ibn al-Jawzi reports al-Dahhak accepts all three second-end views. Al-Damghani also identifies dawn, noon, and afternoon and notes 20:130.

positions.position: Fajr and Asr.
positions.reasons: Razi says sunrise and sunset mark opposite edges, leaving Maghrib to night; he parallels 20:130. Abu Hayyan says each boundary belongs to what it bounds and cites fasting from dawn. Biqai notes morning and afternoon prayer before the Night Journey. Ibn al-Jawzi reports al-Dahhak accepts all three second-end views. Razi says Abu Hanifa inferred later performance of Fajr and Asr near the boundaries.

positions.position: Fajr and Maghrib.
positions.reasons: Tabari argues that all agree on Fajr and that Maghrib alone supplies the opposite end; Wahidi says the apparent wording supports it. Tabrisi says Zuhr and Asr are obvious daytime prayers or specified by 17:78. Qurtubi defends dawn as daytime from fasting law but retains the sunset objection. Kuranyolu defines day as dawn to sunset. Ibn al-Jawzi reports al-Dahhak accepts all three second-end views.

positions.position: Zuhr and Asr are the two boundaries; Fajr is grouped with night prayers.
positions.reasons: Some connect this grouping with quiet versus loud recitation. Elmalili argues dawn is the day's root and noon and afternoon its two prominent parts; the night set of Maghrib, Isha and Fajr gives five prayers, with 17:78 and 20:130.

positions.position: Fajr and Isha.
positions.reasons: Ibn Abi Hatim reports this from Mujahid.

positions.position: Fajr and Zuhr at one end, Asr and Maghrib at the other.
positions.reasons: Wahidi and Baghawi attribute this division to Muqatil.

positions.position: The first end is Fajr, while the evening end remains disputed.
positions.reasons: Tabari says all agree on Fajr but differ about evening; Ibn al-Jawzi reports the majority agrees, but notes Ibn Jarir gives Zuhr instead. Qurtubi transmits Mawardi's claimed agreement and qualifies it by the Zuhr/Asr view. Asad gives the literal wording, 'the two ends of the day.'

turns_on: Whether dawn and sunset count within daytime, and whether the latter half of the day can contain both Zuhr and Asr as an end.

question: Why is the yāʾ of طرفي pronounced with a vowel?

positions.position: It meets a following still consonant and takes the usual kasra.
positions.reasons: Akhfash compares صاحبي السجن at 12:39.

question: Does avoiding major sins already require performing the five prayers?

positions.position: Yes, because abandoning prayer is a major sin.
positions.reasons: Ibn Hajar argues this; al-Alusi says it merits examination.

question: How does al-Tirmidhi grade the principal confession reports?

positions.position: The Ibn Masud account is hasan sahih; the Muadh and Abu al-Yusr routes are weak.
positions.reasons: Ibn Ashur reports al-Tirmidhi's distinctions.

question: Can night prayer erase sins committed during the day?

positions.position: Yes, a believer's night prayer removes daytime sins.
positions.reasons: Tabatabai cites Abu Abdillah and notes parallel transmissions in several collections.

question: What does زلفا mean?

positions.position: Near or successive hours, stages, or portions of the night; singular zulfa.
positions.reasons: Akhfash lists zulfat and zulf as other plurals. Layth and Thalab specify the first night hours; Abu Ubayda, Akhfash and Ibn Qutayba allow any hour. Al-Ajjaj's poem uses successive zulf. Ibn Qutayba and Abu Hayyan derive nearness; Tabari and Mawardi give Muzdalifa etymologies, while Raghib includes rank, favor and euphemistic punishment. Zajjaj rejects an unattested night meaning for zalif. Al-Samarra'i stresses gradual approach and concludes that zulfa conveys drawing near generally.

question: How is زلفا read?

positions.position: Zulafan, with damma on zay and fatha on lam, a plural of zulfa.
positions.reasons: Tabari prefers this because Isha follows portions of the night; Sam in calls it the common reading, and Qurtubi and Abu Hayyan the majority reading. Ibn al-Jazari says the fatha form, like the damma form, is an attested dialectal plural of zulfa, comparing zulam/zulma and yusr/yusra.

positions.position: Zulufan, with damma on both letters.
positions.reasons: Attributed to Medinan readers, Abu Jafar, Ibn Abi Ishaq, Talha and others. Analyses include a plural with vowel harmony, plural of zalif, or dialectal singular; Qiraat-ER says the plural pattern changes without changing meaning. Ibn al-Jazari names Abu Ja'far, Talha, Shayba, Isa ibn Amr and transmitters from Abu Amr for the damma on lam; he treats both vowel forms as dialectal plurals of zulfa.

positions.position: Zulfan, with silent lam.
positions.reasons: Attributed to some Meccan readers and to Ibn Muhaysin and Mujahid. It may shorten the vowelled form or function as a collective singular.

positions.position: Zulfa or zulfa, a singular near interval or rank.
positions.reasons: Mujahid and Ibn Muhaysin transmit the feminine fuʿla form; Kashshaf compares qurba; Sam in calls it a singular adjective for a near rank or hour.

turns_on: The vowel on lam and whether the form is a plural, collective, or singular.

question: How do طرفي النهار and زلفا function grammatically?

positions.position: Both are accusative time expressions governed by establish; زلفا is coordinated with طرفي.
positions.reasons: Kashshaf, Nasafi and Sam in say taraf becomes temporal through annexation to a time, as do 'beginning of day' and 'half of night'; Sam in prefers governance by أقم.

positions.position: The night expressions are prayers that draw one near to God and coordinate with الصلاة.
positions.reasons: Kashshaf supplies the alternative parsing as devotional night prayers; Sam in and Abu Hayyan report it.

positions.position: من الليل modifies زلفا as an adjective.
positions.reasons: Sam in explicitly parses the prepositional phrase as a qualifier.

turns_on: Whether زلفا names a time coordinate with the day ends or a prayer coordinate with الصلاة.

question: Which prayers are meant by the night intervals?

positions.position: Maghrib and Isha.
positions.reasons: Hasan transmits this as the Prophet's description of two night intervals; Tabari lists early authorities. Zajjaj and Wahidi put sunset within night. Al-Samarra'i reports that many commentators identify Maghrib and Isha because their night portions are nearest daytime.

positions.position: Isha alone, in a later portion of night.
positions.reasons: Mujahid calls it an hour at Isha. Ibn Abbas cited the phrase in favor of delaying Isha; Tabari says Isha follows portions of night.

positions.position: Voluntary night vigil or tahajjud.
positions.reasons: Ibn Abi Hatim reports Ibn Abbas's voluntary-night gloss. Ibn Kathir describes the earlier obligation of night vigil and its later abrogation; Bursevi cites 17:79 for the Prophet.

positions.position: Maghrib, Isha, and Fajr.
positions.reasons: The dawn-as-night classification may follow loud recitation; Elmalili argues this yields five prayers.

positions.position: Maghrib, Isha, and witr or night vigil; or Isha, witr, and tahajjud.
positions.reasons: Razi and Elmalili infer at least three from the broken plural; Razi argues witr obligation using 34:20, while Elmalili describes a possible sixth prayer and 17:79. Bursevi reports Abu Hanifa's witr view.

positions.position: Night prayer without specifying which one.
positions.reasons: Qurtubi attributes this to Akhfash. Al-Samarra'i reports an unrestricted reading of night prayer as drawing near to God.

turns_on: Which hours count as night approaches and whether the plural requires at least three prayers.

question: What do the prayer times establish as a legal duty?
words: وَأَقِمِ ٱلصَّلَوٰةَ طَرَفَىِ ٱلنَّهَارِ وَزُلَفًۭا مِّنَ ٱلَّيْلِ

positions.position: They indicate the five obligatory prayers, while prophetic practice supplies their exact times and form.
positions.reasons: Qurtubi cites 16:44 and other prayer verses, the Prophet's 'pray as you have seen me pray,' and completion of religion at 5:3. Elmalili infers five from two day periods and three night periods.

positions.position: Only two daily prayers are obligatory.
positions.reasons: The Kharijites construe the night phrase as an adjective to the day ends and argue the two prayers erase even omission of other prayers.

positions.position: Witr is obligatory as a third night prayer.
positions.reasons: Razi invokes the plural minimum of three and 34:20; Bursevi cites Abu Hanifa; Elmalili says a sixth prayer is probable, so witr is practical wājib rather than a creed obligation.

positions.position: Five established prayers are performed in congregation.
positions.reasons: Elmalili says the call is sunnah and congregational prayer wājib.

turns_on: Whether the plural of night intervals denotes specific obligatory prayers and how much detail the verse itself supplies.

question: What are the good deeds that remove bad deeds?

positions.position: The five prescribed prayers, especially with ablution.
positions.reasons: Tabari prefers this from context and recurrent sound prophetic reports; Ibn al-Jawzi prefers the majority and a connected report. Ka'b, Salman and the Prophet compare prayer to washing dirt or shaking leaves; Uthman says each prayer expiates the interval since the prior prayer.

positions.position: All acts of obedience or accepted good deeds, with prayer as a leading example.
positions.reasons: Ibn Atiyya and Abu Hayyan treat specific deeds as examples of general wording. Alusi adduces reports on voluntary affirmation, fasting Arafat, and gratitude. Qushayri lists nearness, remorse, tears, kindness, generosity, good opinion, sincerity and truthfulness as remedies for particular faults. Bursevi ranks knowledge of God, monotheism and resisting the lower self highly.

positions.position: Remembrance formulas: glorification, praise, testimony of divine unity, and magnification.
positions.reasons: Most reports attribute these to Mujahid, with slight variation: Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu Hayyan include reliance on God; Ata calls them the enduring good works. Abu Dharr's report calls the testimony the best good deed; Bursevi transmits the same answer from the Prophet. Al-Itqan cites Abu Dharr's report naming la ilaha illa Allah as the best good deed.

positions.position: Repentance and return to obedience.
positions.reasons: Jishumi prefers Abu Ali's reading: unbelievers can do good without erasure, so repentance is essential; Tabrisi says repentance certainly cancels punishment.

positions.position: The Prophet's and believers' good actions that overcome polytheists' evil actions.
positions.reasons: This interpretation makes the verse a promise of religious victory; Abu Muslim links it to truth crushing falsehood in 21:18.

turns_on: Whether the definite good deeds refer to the preceding prayer, particular devotions, or the general class of obedience.

question: How do good deeds remove bad deeds?

positions.position: They expiate the guilt, punishment, or effects of earlier sins.
positions.reasons: Abu Hayyan and Bursevi distinguish expiation from making a past act never occur. Alusi says liability is removed; another explanation has records erased. Tabatabai speaks of traces in believers' souls. Ibn Kathir cites ablution and two-unit prayer reports.

positions.position: Regular good deeds help a person stop committing sins.
positions.reasons: Al-Asamm, Kashshaf, Abu Hayyan and Bursevi cite prayer restraining indecency at 29:45; Elmalili adds that regular prayer cultivates remorse for major sins. Ibn Ashur allows both prevention and expiation.

positions.position: God turns sins into good deeds after covering and forgiving them.
positions.reasons: Yahya ibn Muadh cites 25:70.

positions.position: Only good can remove evil; an evil deed cannot.
positions.reasons: The Prophet says illicit wealth is not accepted as charity; Abu Abdillah rejects charity and pilgrimage funded by officials' illicit earnings.

positions.position: Inward light from prayer and remembrance dispels darkness from the senses and bodily life.
positions.reasons: Qashani describes prayer's light removing sensory residue. Bursevi compares sacred works nurturing spirit to a watered seed multiplied seven hundredfold (2:261); Wasiti uses the light-and-darkness image.

positions.position: Recent good deeds overtake older sins.
positions.reasons: Hasan urges meeting old sins with new deeds; Abu Ubayda says even vast sins can be overcome by a good deed. Al-Itqan records a weak Ibn Abbas report in which the Prophet calls a new good deed after an old sin exceptionally quick and effective.

positions.position: Follow a bad deed with a good one as a general moral instruction.
positions.reasons: The Prophet gives this counsel to Muadh and Abu Dharr, alongside fearing God and treating people well. Al-Itqan cites Abu Dharr's report of the Prophet's instruction to follow a bad deed with an erasing good deed.

turns_on: Whether removal means retrospective expiation, prevention of future wrongdoing, or spiritual transformation.

question: Which sins are removed, and on what conditions?

positions.position: Minor sins are expiated if major sins are avoided.
positions.reasons: The prayer report conditions expiation on avoiding majors. Ibn Ashur cites 53:32 and 4:31. Sunni majority make avoidance a condition of the whole promise, while another group treats majors as excluded from what is erased; Alusi prefers that distinction and argues prayers erase minors even when majors exist. Al-Damghani gives minor sins as a sense of sayyi'at that good deeds remove and cites 46:16 for overlooking them.

positions.position: Minor sins require repentance and nonpersistence for erasure.
positions.reasons: Ibn Atiyya invokes sins falling with ablution water and expert legal theorists; Abu Hayyan concurs. Alusi records disagreement and stresses that expiation does not end the duty to repent.

positions.position: Repentance can expiate major sins.
positions.reasons: Jishumi favors Abu Ali's reading; Tabrisi says punishment is cancelled by repentance without dispute. Al-Subki reports debate over whether forgiveness after repentance for sins is certain or presumed.

positions.position: Some good deeds can expiate major as well as minor sins.
positions.reasons: Al-Sadiq says a later good deed can remove a forgotten grave sin. Al-Dhakha'ir cites promises of forgiveness of past and future sins; Ibn al-Mundhir inclines to this. Alusi answers critics who invoke Murji'ism by retaining the duty of repentance.

positions.position: Faith erases unbelief and at least removes eternal punishment, so believers' sins cannot ultimately harm them.
positions.reasons: Razi reports this argument by its proponents.

positions.position: A major sin may be lightened when an expiatory act finds no minor sins.
positions.reasons: Al-Nawawi presents this as a hope.

positions.position: Avoidance of major sins can itself expiate minor sins at each time, when restraint is intentional.
positions.reasons: Al-Balqini reads 4:31 over a lifetime; Alusi rejects that reading with al-Qadi and Ghazali. Ghazali requires ability and desire to commit the major sin.

positions.position: Punishment for minor sins remains possible despite avoidance of majors.
positions.reasons: Alusi reports Sunni authorities citing 4:48 and 18:49; Mu'tazila deny this from 4:31, which may concern unbelief.

turns_on: How to read the condition about major sins and the scope of divine expiation.

question: What happened in the incident linked to this verse?

positions.position: A man had illicit physical contact with a woman short of intercourse, confessed, and the Prophet applied the verse and prayer as expiation.
positions.reasons: Accounts vary: a date seller lured a woman home, a man kissed or touched her backside, or a woman by a pool occasioned temptation. Some say the Prophet waited until revelation; others say Gabriel brought it after Asr. Abu Bakr and Umar advised concealment and repentance. Some reports prescribe thorough ablution and two units, others prayer with the Prophet. Tirmidhi grades Ibn Masud's reports hasan sahih, Abu al-Yusr's hasan gharib with a weak transmitter; Ibn Ashur says Muadh and Abu al-Yusr routes are weak. Ibn Abi Hatim and Durr preserve other versions. Al-Burhan reports a date seller who tried to seduce a buyer; its Ibn Mas'ud report in both Sahihs describes a kiss followed by the Prophet's application of this verse.

positions.position: The pool encounter ended in remorse, with forgiveness sought and four prayer units prescribed.
positions.reasons: Ibn Kathir calls Yahya ibn Ja'da's account mursal. The reports differ on whether the man found a woman by a pool or approached her while she bathed, and whether impotence stopped him.

positions.position: The verse already existed, and the Prophet applied its general rule to the penitent.
positions.reasons: Ibn Ashur cites a Tirmidhi transmission saying the Prophet recited the verse without saying it newly descended; 'revealed' can mean applied to the case.

positions.position: The verse was newly revealed in response to the confession.
positions.reasons: The Prophet's silence or delay until revelation is a recurrent detail; Ibn Ashur notes this wording would make the verse Medinan.

positions.position: The verse descended again when a new incident arose, recalling its existing ruling.
positions.reasons: Al-Burhan says an already revealed verse may recur when a new case prompts it; this explains a report of revelation without requiring the first descent then.

turns_on: Whether the reports describe new revelation or application of an existing verse, and the varying details of the man's act and remedy.

question: Who was the man in the confession report?

positions.position: Abu al-Yusr, the Ansari date seller; names given include Amr ibn Ghaziya and Ka'b ibn Amr.
positions.reasons: Mawardi, Ibn al-Jawzi and Ibn Kathir preserve divergent personal names for Abu al-Yusr. Tirmidhi's Abu al-Yusr transmission is reported as hasan gharib, with Qays ibn al-Rabi weakened. Al-Burhan says al-Tirmidhi or another source identifies the confessor as Abu al-Yusr.

positions.position: Abu Miqbal or Abu Nufayl, Amir ibn Qays al-Ansari.
positions.reasons: Muqatil gives Abu Miqbal Amir ibn Qays of Banu al-Najjar; Ibn Kathir quotes Abu Nufayl as a variant.

positions.position: An Ansari named Flan ibn Muattib or Ibn Muqib.
positions.reasons: Ibrahim's reports supply these differing forms.

positions.position: A man of Banu Ghanm or Banu Tamim.
positions.reasons: Yazid ibn Ruman's transmitted tribal designations vary.

positions.position: Nabhan al-Tammar.
positions.reasons: Abu Hayyan reports this identification for the good-deeds clause.

positions.position: An Ansari called Abbad.
positions.reasons: Reported as an alternative identification.

positions.position: The report leaves the man unnamed.
positions.reasons: These accounts describe his conduct without a name.

positions.position: Abu Miqbal al-Husayn ibn Umar ibn Qays, the date seller.
positions.reasons: Al-Burhan transmits this fuller and different name for the man who tried to seduce a woman buying dates.

turns_on: Variant transmission of the man's name, kunya, and tribe.

question: To whom did the Prophet say the verse's remedy applies?

positions.position: It applies generally to all believers or the Prophet's community who act on it.
positions.reasons: The questioner is variously Umar, Muadh, or Abu al-Yusr (Ibn al-Jawzi). The Prophet's answers uniformly make the remedy general; al-Alusi says the occasion does not restrict the wording. Al-Burhan's Ibn Mas'ud report explicitly says the Prophet extended the ruling to the whole community.

question: What legal consequence follows for an unlawful kiss or touch?

positions.position: It does not incur the fixed penalty for intercourse.
positions.reasons: Qurtubi infers this from the incident and expiation through prayer.

positions.position: Even a man and woman found in one garment incur neither a fixed penalty nor discretionary punishment.
positions.reasons: Ibn al-Mundhir is reported to choose this on the basis of the incident.

question: What is the grammatical form of ذكرى?

positions.position: It is a verbal noun ending in feminine alif, with other attested forms and a plural.
positions.reasons: Abu Ali compares العدوى, الدعوى and شورى; Sibawayh records الذكر with dal and cites Ibn Muqbil's line, alongside 12:45. Qurtubi calls it a verbal noun.

question: To what does ذلك point?

positions.position: The preceding counsel and commands, including steadfastness and prayer.
positions.reasons: Kashshaf starts at the uprightness command; Tabari includes this surah's commands and prohibitions. Ibn Atiyya and Ibn al-Jawzi mention avoiding transgression and unjust rulers; Biqai includes warning and consolation.

positions.position: The command to establish prayer at these times.
positions.reasons: Abu Hayyan prefers the nearest antecedent; Ibn Atiyya says prayer supplies a cause and setting for remembrance.

positions.position: The statement or promise that good deeds erase sins.
positions.reasons: Ibn Atiyya says this encourages good deeds; Jishumi calls it the promise itself.

positions.position: The Qur'an.
positions.reasons: Wahidi says it is an admonition for one who remembers the Quran.

positions.position: This, meaning the present admonition.
positions.reasons: Ibn Abbas takes ذلك in the sense of هذا.

question: Who benefits from the reminder, and what kind of reminder is it?

positions.position: It is admonition for people who remember God and heed it.
positions.reasons: Tabari contrasts responsive people with sealed hearts and mentions hope for reward and fear of warning. Hasan describes remembering in prosperity, adversity, health and illness; Mujahid adds standing, sitting and lying. Alusi and Qurtubi say those who heed are named because they benefit.

positions.position: It is a call to repentance or recollection of one's own sin.
positions.reasons: Al-Kalbi calls it repentance; Yazid ibn Ruman and Ibn Jurayj say the penitent man continued to remember his deed.

positions.position: It strengthens believers in religion.
positions.reasons: Abu Muslim explains the reminder's effect this way.

positions.position: It recalls spiritual clarity, gathered attention, intimacy and taste.
positions.reasons: Both connect prayer times and sins' removal to inward recollection.

turns_on: Whether the reminder is admonition, repentance, doctrinal strengthening, or inward recollection.

question: How does the verse connect to nearby commands and other verses?

positions.position: Prayer follows the command to remain upright as the foremost aid to steadfastness, and its expiatory power explains the command.
positions.reasons: Ibn Ashur says 'indeed' emphasizes the causal explanation and links 29:45; Biqai says prayer cures the weakness behind lesser sins.

positions.position: Other verses supply or parallel these prayer times.
positions.reasons: Muqatil recalls Moses' prayer for remembrance at 20:14; Hasan invokes 17:78; Razi and Elmalili cite 20:130; Bursevi adds 50:39–40. Study Quran compares disagreement over the middle prayer at 2:238.

positions.position: The verse's direct address to the Prophet marks positive commands, while prohibitions address the community.
positions.reasons: Elmalili says this shift implies transgression and inclination to oppressors are conceivable for the community, not the Prophet.

question: Was this verse revealed in Mecca or Medina?

positions.position: It was revealed in Medina as an exception within the surah.
positions.reasons: Ibn Abbas and Qatada infer this from the confession report's 'revealed to him' wording; many commentators list verses 12, 17 and 114 as possible exceptions. Al-Itqan lists this verse among three Medinan exceptions in Hud and supports its dating with several sound routes about Abu al-Yusr.

positions.position: It is Meccan along with the whole surah; the Prophet later applied it to the penitent.
positions.reasons: Rashid Rida rejects Medina dating as unconvincing. Ibn Kathir suggests it may predate the five prayers of the Night Journey, when two daily prayers and night vigil were required.

positions.position: If newly revealed in Medina, it was placed here for coherence with steadfastness and patience.
positions.reasons: Ibn Ashur points to the adjacent commands at 11:112 and 11:115.

positions.position: It descended twice, first in Mecca and then in Medina.
positions.reasons: Al-Burhan and al-Zarkashi in al-Itqan use repeated descent to reconcile the Meccan status of Hud with the Medinan confession report; recurrence magnifies and renews a verse.

turns_on: Whether 'revealed' in the confession account denotes first revelation or application of an earlier verse.

question: What distinct reports illustrate the verse's hope and expiation?

positions.position: The five prayers wash away sins like repeated bathing in a river or leaves falling from a branch.
positions.reasons: Salman shakes a dry branch; the Prophet's river image asks whether dirt could remain after five baths. Tabatabai lists parallel Sunni transmissions.

positions.position: It is the most hopeful verse, according to a report from Ali and the Prophet.
positions.reasons: Ali rejects proposed alternatives at 4:48 and 4:110 before identifying this prayer command.

positions.position: God's mercy to a believer exceeds a mother bird's care for her chick.
positions.reasons: The Prophet uses the bird's entrusted chick as the comparison.

positions.position: A worshiper who makes people despair of mercy is himself made to despair after death.
positions.reasons: Zayd ibn Aslam transmits the warning.

positions.position: Ablution itself purifies and draws immense reward.
positions.reasons: Bursevi notes jurists who treated used ablution cloth as impure because sins wash off; the Moses report promises a garden per drop, and Hafiz praises prayer purified by tears.

positions.position: Faith and lawful deeds matter: illicit wealth is not blessed or accepted as charity.
positions.reasons: The Prophet says faith is given to those God loves and requires a surrendered heart and tongue and a safe neighbor.

positions.position: Testimony of faith can erase sins, though some specific routes are weak or unique.
positions.reasons: Ibn Kathir notes Uthman al-Waqqasi is weak in one Anas route and another route is unique through Mastur. Abu Dharr's report in al-Itqan identifies the testimony of unity as the best good deed.

positions.position: Every deed is recorded, so one should not belittle a sin or a good deed.
positions.reasons: Al-Sadiq warns of angels recording public and hidden acts.

positions.position: A later good deed swiftly overtakes an old sin.
positions.reasons: Al-Itqan transmits this image from a weak Ibn Abbas report attributed to the Prophet.

question: What inward reading does the verse support?

positions.position: Prayer and remembrance bring light that clears sensory darkness and sustains presence.
positions.reasons: Qashani relates five prayers to five senses and night vigil to refining natural powers; Bursevi describes the luminous spirit nourished by good works, and Wasiti contrasts obedience's light with sin's darkness. The Study Quran reports a heart polished by remembrance (13:28).

question: What senses can al-sayyi'at have in Quranic usage?

positions.position: Bad deeds, the opposite of good deeds.
positions.reasons: Ibn al-Jawzi gives the basic contrast.

positions.position: Associating partners with God.
positions.reasons: Ibn al-Jawzi reports this Quranic use at 4:18 and 10:27.

positions.position: Punishment or the consequences of wrongdoing.
positions.reasons: Ibn al-Jawzi reports this use at 39:51.

positions.position: Harm or misfortune.
positions.reasons: Ibn al-Jawzi cites afflictions in 7:168 and 11:10.

positions.position: Evil or wicked schemes.
positions.reasons: Ibn al-Jawzi reports this sense at 40:45.

positions.position: Men having sex with men.
positions.reasons: Ibn al-Jawzi reports this use in the account of Lot's people at 11:78.

turns_on: The word's sense changes with its Quranic context; these parallels do not all interpret its occurrence here.

question: How is the ta in الصلاة طرفي pronounced in large assimilation?

positions.position: The ta assimilates into the following emphatic ta.
positions.reasons: Al-Itqan lists this exact phrase; Ibn al-Jazari reports that most performance authorities favor assimilation for homorganicity and the strength of the following consonant.

positions.position: Al-Susi clearly articulates the ta in one reported route.
positions.reasons: Ibn Habash alone reports this from al-Susi, citing the light vowel and preceding still consonant; Ibn al-Jazari notes other authorities' assimilation.

turns_on: The exceptional transmission from al-Susi versus other performance authorities.

question: What large assimilation is cited at السيئات ذلك?

positions.position: The final ta is assimilated before dhal.
positions.reasons: Ibn al-Jazari lists this exact join among nine instances of assimilation before dhal.

question: Which supplied notes do not interpret this verse?

positions.position: Several excerpts concern other grammar, rhetoric, biography, theology, recitation, and abrogation topics without explaining 11:114.
